title: JWT Expiry and Verification: exp, Clock Skew, and Common Myths
description: JWT exp, nbf and iat are NumericDate seconds. Compare expiry with server time and a few minutes of skew; decoding or HS256 verification is no proof of validity.
content:
JWT's exp is a NumericDate in seconds. Deciding whether a token has expired means comparing the server's current time with exp, and a few minutes of clock skew can be allowed. Decoding only reads Header and Payload, and HS256 verification only shows that the signature matches; none of the three stands in for another.

1. First, tell three things apart: decoding, verification, claim validation

Paste a JWT into the tool and press the decode button: what you see is the JSON of the Header and Payload. Press the HS256 verification button and the tool recomputes an HMAC with the key you typed and compares it with the third segment. Neither action is a complete proof that the token is valid.

  • Decoding: Base64URL conversion restores the JSON, which proves that the string splits into three segments and that the first two are valid JSON.
  • Verification: recomputing the signature with a key proves that "the signature matches this header.payload".
  • Claim validation: checking exp, nbf, iss, aud, revocation status, and permissions decides "whether this token can be used right now".

This site's JWT decoder puts the first two steps on one page: it decodes, and it verifies with an HS256 key. It renders exp into a summary yet never rejects a token for being expired. So the green 「解码成功」 ("decode succeeded") on the page only means parsing succeeded; it does not mean a server would accept the token.

2. The three segments: Header, Payload, Signature

RFC 7519 describes a JWT as URL-safe segments separated by periods, each segment a base64url-encoded value. A JWT in JWS form usually has exactly three segments: the Header describes the algorithm and type, the Payload carries the claims, and the Signature protects the first two.

The base64url in a three-segment JWS is not encryption: it only swaps the Base64 characters + and / for - and _, and strips trailing = padding. Anyone holding the token can restore the plaintext JSON, so do not put passwords, long-term keys, or personal data the client should not read into the Payload. To compare the two encodings side by side, the Base64 encoder and decoder show both outputs for the same bytes.

SegmentTypical contentReadable directly?How this site's tool shows it
Header{"alg":"HS256","typ":"JWT"}Yes, just Base64URL-decode it「═══ Header ═══」 plus indented JSON
Payloadclaims such as sub, iat, exp, issYes, not encrypted by default「═══ Payload ═══」 plus indented JSON
Signaturea signature or MAC over header.payloadNo, but it can be recomputed and comparedNot expanded separately in the output; used during verification

The signature input is not the whole token but ASCII(BASE64URL(header) || '.' || BASE64URL(payload)); the third segment is not part of it. RFC 7515 section 5.2 also requires alg to be present and to name the algorithm actually used.

3. exp, iat, nbf: the unit is seconds, not milliseconds

A NumericDate is defined as the number of seconds elapsed since 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z, and non-integer values are allowed. RFC 7519 requires exp, nbf, and iat to be of this type: exp means "must not be accepted at or after this time", nbf means "must not be accepted before this time", and iat only records the issue time, which can be used to judge the token's age.

That is why exp is usually a 10-digit number. Feed a 13-digit millisecond value in and the tool still reads it as seconds: the page multiplies exp by 1000 before constructing a date, so a 13-digit value pushes the year to five digits and looks like "never expires". To convert a timestamp, use the timestamp converter to confirm the unit first.

All three claims are marked OPTIONAL: without exp a token is not necessarily permanent, it only means the standard sets no cutoff, and the server can still invalidate it through session policy, key rotation, and revocation.

4. Clock skew: a few minutes of tolerance, not a permanent pass

The issuer, the resource server, and the verifier may not be the same machine, and system clocks drift slightly. RFC 7519 allows implementations a little leeway for exp and nbf, usually no more than a few minutes, to absorb that clock skew; it is not a reason to push the expiry out indefinitely.

A decoder running in the browser uses the local clock: the page computes the remaining minutes with Date.now() and formats dates with toLocaleString in the local time zone. A laptop clock that is ten minutes slow adds ten minutes to "N minutes left", and another time zone shows another wall-clock hour. None of this changes the judgement the server makes with its own clock.

So "it has not expired locally" cannot be the basis for authorization. The server should set an acceptable offset from its own clock and policy; a client-side display is only good for troubleshooting.

5. Checking the time claims in this site's JWT decoder

The steps are simple: press 「示例」 ("sample") to load the built-in token, then press 「解码」 ("decode"). The output area shows the Header and Payload first, then a summary section: the exp line carries the local time and remaining minutes, the iat line gives the issue time, and sub and iss each add a line when present. The status bar turns green and reports success.

This sample token's Header is {"alg":"HS256","typ":"JWT"}, its Payload is {"sub":"clover","iat":1785000000,"exp":1816536000}, and the third segment is the Base64URL of the 18-byte AnExampleSignature. That is not a 32-byte HMAC-SHA256 result, so after entering any non-empty key and pressing the verify button the page always returns "signature invalid"; the sample exists to show the structure, not to be a verifiable specimen.

One more easy misreading: decode a token that has already expired and the page still reports a successful decode, noting "expired" only in the summary. The status bar describes the parse result, not the expiry conclusion; that is exactly why a successful decode is not a valid token.

6. HS256 verification: it only answers whether this key produces the same signature

Verification needs both a token and a key. Once both are non-empty the page splits the token into three segments, confirms that alg is HS256, recomputes HMAC-SHA256 over header.payload with the key, converts the result to Base64URL, and compares it character by character with the third segment; a match shows a green success status, a mismatch shows the same error message for both a wrong key and a tampered token.

"Signature valid" only proves that the signature matches; it does not prove the token is unexpired, the issuer is trusted, the audience is right, or the token is unrevoked. A wrong key and a tampered Payload produce the same failure text, and the page does not distinguish them, so you cannot tell from it whether the key is wrong or the content was changed. If the Header's alg is not HS256, the page shows a notice that the tool only verifies HS256 and that this token uses RS256, then stops; it will not fall back to another algorithm.

The page uppercases alg before comparing, so a lowercase spelling such as hs256 also passes; a server should not depend on that loose matching but should whitelist exact algorithm names and key types from the registry.

7. HS256 vs RS256: different key directions, and the token does not choose the algorithm

HS256 is a symmetric MAC: the same shared key signs and verifies, which suits a single service or a controlled group of services. RS256 is asymmetric: a private key signs and a public key verifies, so a resource server can verify with only the public key and the private key need not be distributed to every verification point. This is a difference in key distribution model, not a simple ranking of strength.

The key risk is algorithm confusion: the alg in the Header is written by the sender, so an attacker can change it. RFC 8725 section 2.1 names attacks that change alg to none, or change RS256 to HS256 and use the RSA public key as the HMAC key; the matching best practices are that the caller specifies the allowed algorithm set and each key is used for one algorithm only (section 3.1), and that only algorithms meeting current security requirements are accepted (section 3.2).

So a server should decide from its business rules that "only RS256 is accepted here", then verify with the corresponding public key; it must not verify whatever the Header says, still less treat a public key as an HS256 shared secret. This site's tool supporting only HS256 is a boundary of the local demo, not a template for server implementations.

8. Revocation, a missing exp, and "does decoding mean it is valid?"

A token can be revoked even when the signature is correct and the time has not passed. OAuth 2.0 token revocation requires implementations to support refresh token revocation and recommends access token revocation; after the revocation endpoint receives a request the token is invalid immediately, though a real deployment may see propagation delay. For self-contained access tokens the spec also acknowledges that backend interaction between the authorization server and the resource server may be needed, or that short-lived tokens should be used to shrink the window.

Issuer and audience must be checked as well: iss identifies the issuer, and how to handle it is left to the application; aud identifies the intended recipient, and a processor that is not in the audience must reject the token. RFC 8725 sections 3.8 and 3.9 list "validate issuer and subject" and "validate audience" as separate requirements. When replay protection is needed, jti can serve as a unique identifier alongside server-side records.

  1. Verify with a fixed algorithm whitelist, and confirm that the key really belongs to that issuer.
  2. Check exp and nbf against the server's current time, allowing only the small offset the policy permits.
  3. Check that iss, aud, and sub match the current application and user.
  4. Check whether the session or token was revoked, logged out, or rotated, consulting jti or a version number where needed.
  5. Only then do permissions and business authorization; a signature only settles "the content was not changed", not "this person may do this".

Back to the common question: a successful decode means the three segments split and the first two are valid JSON; a successful verification means the signature matches. Neither equals "the token is valid". Only after signature, time, issuer, audience, revocation, and permissions are all checked do you have a usable authorization conclusion.

9. Boundaries and limits: what a local tool can and cannot do

This site's JWT decoder handles only the three-segment JWS compact form; it does not handle five-segment JWE or parse encrypted content, and verification supports only HS256, not RS256, ES256, or other algorithms. It shows an exp summary but does not enforce expiry, and it does not validate aud, iss, or revocation. The sample token's signature is an 18-byte demo value and cannot pass HS256 verification.

Processing does stay local: in this test run no request carrying the token appeared during decoding, and the key box says 「仅本地校验，不离开浏览器」 ("local verification only, never leaves the browser"). But "local" is not "safe to paste anything": screenshots, screen recordings, browser extensions, and shared machines can all leak a token. Use a redacted test token and never paste production credentials.

Two smaller boundaries: the clear button only clears the input and output and hides the status bar, while the key box keeps its previous value; dates are displayed in the browser's local time zone, so the same token shows different clock times in different zones. Keeping these two points in mind saves some "why does it differ from the server" confusion.

The normative parts of this article follow RFC 7519, RFC 7515, RFC 8725, and RFC 7009; page behavior follows the current live implementation and the evidence from this test run; the times and states in the examples were reproduced with a fixed clock.

faqs.q: Does a successful JWT decode mean the token is valid?
faqs.a: No. Decoding only restores Base64URL and parses JSON; the signature, exp/nbf, iss/aud, revocation status, and permissions all have to be checked separately. This site's tool still shows 「解码成功」 ("decode succeeded") for an expired token, marking it as expired only in the summary.

faqs.q: Is exp in seconds or milliseconds?
faqs.a: RFC 7519 defines exp as a NumericDate in seconds since 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z, and non-integer values are allowed. This site's tool multiplies exp by 1000 before building a date; a 13-digit millisecond value is read as seconds and pushes the year to five digits. With an unusual implementation, check the issuer's documentation first.

faqs.q: Can a wrong local clock or a different time zone change the expiry decision?
faqs.a: They affect the "N minutes left" and the dates you see in the browser, because the page computes and displays them with Date.now() and the local time zone; the server should judge by its own clock and a small allowed leeway. Never make an authorization decision from a client-side display.

faqs.q: What is the difference between HS256 and RS256?
faqs.a: HS256 is an HMAC with one shared key, so both the issuer and the verifier must hold it; RS256 signs with a private key and verifies with a public key, so a resource server needs only the public key. A server should fix the set of allowed algorithms rather than switching algorithm based on the Header's alg, and must not use an RSA public key as an HS256 secret.

faqs.q: If a token has no exp, is it permanent?
faqs.a: No. RFC 7519 marks exp as OPTIONAL; without it the standard simply sets no cutoff. A server can still invalidate the token through session policy, short lifetimes, key rotation, a revocation list, or a record keyed by jti.

faqs.q: Can a revoked token be spotted by decoding or verifying it?
faqs.a: No. A JWT usually carries no revocation state, and a token whose signature and exp are both fine may already be revoked. OAuth 2.0 defines a revocation endpoint, but a self-contained token often needs a backend call or a shorter lifetime; the issuer's session or revocation records decide the answer.
